title: Different Schools, Different Futures
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard argues that schools should stop waiting for a stable, consistent approach to AI and instead expect and accept divergent policies and institutions. Treating AI as an implementation problem avoids the larger question of what happens when change outruns the systems that prepare people for it. He questions whether traditional assignments and credentials still prove what they claim, and he foresees more varied pathways such as microschools, mentors and lifelong return to education. He weighs the historical objection of tracking and the need for a common knowledge foundation, insisting that access must be equitable. The move is to reframe AI policy debates as a prompt to reconsider the purpose of schooling.
points: Schools are waiting for a period of stability that may never arrive, and AI policy cannot be treated as a problem a faculty meeting can resolve.
If AI can produce the essay and pass the exam, schools must explain what success on those tasks demonstrates and why students need to do them without AI.
Education is likely to become more varied in form and content, from microschools to public schools acting as coordinating institutions.
Pathways differ from tracks in who chooses them, whether they can be left, and whether they sit on a common foundation.
Equal access is essential, since high-poverty districts lag in AI teacher training, and education will increasingly need to be lifelong.
quotes: We are waiting for a period of stability that may never arrive. We are treating the early stages of a continuing transformation as an implementation problem that a sufficiently thorough faculty meeting can resolve.
The question that should bother us is a different one: what happens when the world changes faster than the systems responsible for preparing people to live in it?
A school can be extremely consistent about preparing students for a world that is disappearing.

Teaching people and sorting people are different activities. A system can become very good at sorting students while becoming less useful at preparing them for what follows. AI puts pressure on that distinction.
The difference between a pathway and a track is who chooses it, whether it can be left, and where it leads. A track is assigned early and narrows what comes after.

A smaller school teaching the same curriculum through the same assignments is a smaller version of the existing model. A personalized system that helps everyone reach the same predetermined answers more efficiently changes the pace more than the purpose.

Greater diversity of educational pathways needs to come with meaningful access. Public investment, reliable institutions, qualified educators, and opportunities for shared civic life will matter enormously.
Students will need to learn, reconsider, build, abandon, and begin again.
